```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE)
```

This article shows how to plot smooths fitted with {scam}, extract estimates and
intervals, sample fitted functions, and check predictions. We use increasing
effects of two covariates to illustrate these operations. {gratia} also supports
scam's other one- and two-dimensional shape-constrained smooths and ordinary
{mgcv} smooths fitted through `scam()`.

We load gratia and scam before simulating the example.
```{r packages}
library("gratia")
load_mgcv()
library("scam")
```

The response below combines an increasing curved effect of `x` and a linear
effect of `z`, with independent Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.15.
The covariates are independently sampled on the unit interval.
```{r simulate-data}
set.seed(46)
d <- data.frame(x = runif(200), z = runif(200))
d$y <- exp(d$x) + d$z + rnorm(nrow(d), sd = 0.15)
```

We fit increasing smooths for both covariates and plot their estimated contributions.
```{r fit-model}
m <- scam(y ~ s(x, bs = "mpi", k = 8) + s(z, bs = "mpi", k = 8),
  data = d, not.exp = TRUE)
draw(m)
```

## Plot smooth contributions

The captions identify the spline basis and its shape constraints. Arrows
indicate increasing or decreasing effects. For a tensor product smooth,
the caption identifies the constraint on each covariate. The same captions
appear when drawing estimates saved with `smooth_estimates()`.

By default, `draw()` uses the fitted smooth's centring, so the plotted value
at a given location stays the same if you change the evaluation grid.
For bivariate smooths, scam subtracts the average across the plotted grid.
Use `centre = "plot"` to match that convention in `draw()` or `assemble()`.
The following example fits a surface that increases with both covariates and
centres it on the plotted grid.

```{r surface}
b <- scam(y ~ s(x, z, bs = "tedmi", k = c(5, 5)), data = d,
  not.exp = TRUE)
draw(b, centre = "plot", n_2d = 40)
```

For univariate smooths, scam uses two standard errors for its default limits.
gratia uses `qnorm(0.975)` for 95% normal limits. The packages can also
calculate different standard errors for the same curve. gratia uses the
derivative of the plotted function with respect to the fitted coefficients
to calculate how their uncertainty affects the curve.

## Estimate intervals, derivatives and sampled functions

For intervals and derivatives, gratia uses the covariance of the coefficients
after scam applies its shape constraints. The intervals use local normal
approximations, with the smoothing parameters held at their fitted values.
`frequentist = TRUE` selects the frequentist covariance. Use
`overall_uncertainty = FALSE` to leave out the intercept's uncertainty.
First extract pointwise
smooth intervals, estimate the slope of the `x` smooth, and request a
simultaneous band for that smooth. A simultaneous band describes uncertainty
over the evaluated curve, whereas the pointwise limits apply to each location
separately.

```{r estimates}
e <- smooth_estimates(m, overall_uncertainty = FALSE)
e <- add_confint(e)
head(e)
derivatives(m, select = "s(x)")
confint(m, parm = "s(x)", type = "simultaneous", seed = 53)
```

scam fits unconstrained parameters and transforms some of them to positive
coefficients to enforce the smooth's shape. Coefficient sampling draws from a
normal approximation for those unconstrained parameters, then applies the same
transformation. This preserves the shape constraints in every sampled curve.
Because the transformation is nonlinear, the samples and the analytic
intervals use different uncertainty approximations. In particular, the
endpoints of an analytic interval need not satisfy the fitted shape constraint.

Use `gaussian_draws()` to obtain a matrix with one coefficient vector per row.
Check its dimensions to confirm the number of draws and coefficients.
`smooth_samples()` evaluates sampled smooth curves directly. We produce five
draws of each smooth and plot them with `draw()` to see how the curves vary
while retaining the fitted shape constraints.

```{r samples}
draws <- gaussian_draws(m, n_draws = 100, seed = 54)
dim(draws)
samples <- smooth_samples(m, n_draws = 5, seed = 55)
head(samples)
draw(samples)
```

The `.smooth` column identifies the smooth, `.draw` identifies the coefficient
draw, and `.value` gives the sampled function's value at each covariate value.
Fitted, derivative and response sampling functions use the same coefficient
transformation. See `smooth_samples()` and
`gaussian_draws()` for the returned columns and options for supplying your
own coefficient draws.

## Predictions and model checks

To predict the mean response as `x` varies, use `conditional_values()`. It
combines both smooths and the intercept, holding `z` at the observed value
closest to its median. The bands show uncertainty in the mean response.

```{r conditional-predictions}
predictions <- conditional_values(m, condition = "x")
predictions
draw(predictions)
```

Use `appraise()` to check how the model describes the observed responses.
Here, quantile residuals compare each observation with its fitted Gaussian
distribution. Look for departures from the reference line in the QQ plot
and for changes in the spread of residuals across the linear predictor.

```{r model-checks}
appraise(m, type = "quantile", seed = 56)
```

The [model diagnostics article](model-checking.html) explains how to interpret
the panels and their reference bands.

## Other GAM operations

Many gratia methods for GAMs also work with scam fits, including smooth
differences, response derivatives and concurvity. For custom predictions,
`lp_matrix()` and `model.matrix()` return a model matrix whose columns
match `coef(m)`. When predicting with new data, gratia reuses any constants
estimated when evaluating formula terms, such as means from `scale()`, and
evaluates offsets specified in the formula. Predictions at the original
observations also retain offsets supplied through the `offset` argument.

For supported response families with independent observations, leave-one-out
cross-validation (LOO) and WAIC use the coefficient sampling approximation
described above. Smoothing parameters and other fitted family parameters
stay fixed. `variance_comp()` reports the fitted response scale divided by
each smoothing parameter. These ratios describe the penalties on the
coefficients before transformation.

For Gaussian identity-link fits with AR1 dependence, response simulation uses
the fitted correlation and `AR.start` series boundaries, including observation
weights. Supply the original observations so that the simulator can use
their order and series boundaries. For other families, scam's working AR1
correction alone does not define a joint response distribution. The
likelihood methods for independent observations require a fit without
AR1 dependence.

For GCV and UBRE fits, the covariance needed to include smoothing parameter
uncertainty is unavailable. If you request `model_edf(type = "unconditional")`
for these fits, gratia warns and returns the usual effective degrees of
freedom. Confidence limits for the penalty-based variance components and
MH and INLA coefficient sampling are unavailable for scam fits. To impose
a supported shape restriction on an interval for a scam smooth, supply
estimates and a grid directly to `shape_intervals()`.
